summary: Henri Maspero worked in sinology, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied at Paris lycées, INALCO, and the EFEO, learning under Sylvain Lévi and Édouard Chavannes. His posts included the EFEO (1908–1920), Collège de France (1919–1944), and EPHE (~1930–1945).

Henri Massé was a scholar in Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics. He held posts at the University of Algiers (~1916–1927) and the École nationale des langues orientales vivantes (~1927–1958).
Henri Seyrig was a historian and archaeologist who studied at the University of Paris (~1919–1922). He served as the head of the Institut français du Proche-Orient from ~1946 to 1967.
Henri d'Ollone was a scholar in sinology and tibetology who received his military education at the École spéciale militaire de Saint-Cyr (~1890–1892).

Henri de Lubac worked in religious and Buddhist studies. He earned a Dr.theol. from the Pontifical Gregorian University and held posts at the Théologat de Fourvière (~1929–1950) and as professor at the Catholic University of Lyon (1929–1961).

Henriette Johanna Wilhelmina Salomons was an Indologist. She studied under Christianus Cornelis Uhlenbeck at Leiden University (B.A. 1901) and under Willem Caland at Utrecht University (Ph.D. ~1906–1913), later lecturing in Dutch at the University of Copenhagen (1928–1929).

Henrik Barić worked in linguistics. He studied under Rudolf Meringer at the University of Graz and earned his Ph.D. at the University of Vienna. He held professorships at the Universities of Belgrade and Sarajevo, and directed the Institute of Balkan Studies.

Henrik Samuel Nyberg specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied at Uppsala University (Ph.D. 1919) under Johansson, Zetterstéen, Danielsson, and Persson, later serving there as docent and professor of Semitic languages (1919; 1931–1956).
Henrik Zilliacus was a scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Helsinki (~1926–1936) and later held a post there (~1944–1974).
Henry Alfred Whitehead worked in religious studies and Indology. He studied at Trinity College, Oxford (~1873–1877) and served as principal of Bishop's College, Calcutta (~1883–1899).

Henry Baily Wade Garrick worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. After studying at the Royal College of Art, he served as an assistant in the Archaeological Survey of India (1880–1890) and as an artist for the Geological Survey of India (1891–1911).

Henry Beveridge was an Indologist and historian who studied at the University of Glasgow (~1853–1856) and Queen's University Belfast (1856). He served in the Indian Civil Service (1857–1893) and was president of The Asiatic Society (1890–1891).
Henry Bower was a scholar of Indology and linguistics who studied at Vepery Seminary. He later served as the Principal Tamil examiner at the University of Madras.

Henry Chung-hung Shiu works in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He earned a PhD from the University of Toronto (-2006) and studied under Shek-Wing Tam, Leonard Priestley, David Waterhouse, and Willard Gurdon Oxtoby, later holding a post at Emmanuel College, Toronto.

Henry Clarke Warren worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He studied at Harvard, Johns Hopkins, and Oxford under Lanman, Palmer, Greenough, Bloomfield, and Davids, and co-founded the Pali Text Society and Harvard Oriental Series.

Henry Cousens was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Archaeological Survey of India as an assistant beginning in 1881 and as Superintendent of Western India from 1891 to 1910.

Henry Creswicke Rawlinson worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, and archaeology. Educated at Great Ealing School and Middlesex University, he held posts with the East India Company, the Foreign Office, and served as Director of the Royal Asiatic Society.

Henry Drummond Williamson was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at Corpus Christi College, University of Cambridge (~1874–1889), and served as a missionary for the Church Missionary Society (1877–1893).

Henry George Briggs worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. His posts included Assistant Secretary at the Great Indian Peninsula Railway (1856), Secretary at the Bombay Municipal Corporation (1860–1862), and a role in the Public Works Department.

Henry George Keene worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies and Indology. He studied at Fort William, Wadham, East India Company, and Sidney Sussex colleges, later serving as Professor of Arabic and Persian at East India Company College (1824–1834).
